edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh XXVII

source_text: Habemus etiam vestimentorum in Scripturis mentionem ad spem carnis allegorizare, quia et Apocalypsis Joannis: Hi sunt, ait, qui vestimenta sua non coinquinaverunt cum mulieribus; virgines scilicet significans, et qui semetipsos castraverunt propter regna coelorum. Itaque in albis erunt vestibus, id est, in claritate innubae carnis. Et in Evangelio, indumentum nuptiale sanctitas carnis agnosci potest. Itaque Esaias docens, quale jejunium elegerit Dominus, cum subjicit de mercede bonitatis: Tunc, inquit, lumen tuum temporaneum erumpet, et vestimenta tua citius orientur: non subsericam utique, nec pallium, sed carnem volens accipi, ortum carnis resurrecturae de mortis occasu praedicavit. Adeo nobis quoque suppetit allegorica defensio corporalis resurrectionis. Nam et cum legimus: Populus meus, introite in cellas promas quantulum, donec ira mea praetereat, sepulcra erunt cellae promae, in quibus paulisper requiescere habebunt, qui in finibus saeculi, sub ultima ira, per Antichristi vim excesserint. Aut cur cellarum promarum potius vocabulo usus est, et non alicujus loci receptorii, nisi quia in cellis promis caro salita et usui reposita servatur, depromenda illinc suo tempore? Proinde enim et corpora medicata condimentis sepulturae, mausoleis et monumentis sequestrantur, processura inde cum jusserit Dominus. Quod cum ita intelligi congruat; et quae enim ab ira Dei cellariorum nos refugia servabunt? hoc ipso quod ait, donec ira praetereat, quae extinguet Antichristum, post iram ostendit processuram carnem de sepulcro, in quo ante iram fuerit illata. Nam et de cellariis non aliud effertur, quam quod infertur; et post Antichristi eradicationem agitabitur resurrectio.
pass_a_gloss: We also have a mention of garments in the Scriptures to allegorize the hope of the flesh, because also the Apocalypse of John says: These are, it says, who have not defiled their garments with women; certainly signifying virgins, and those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the heavenly kingdoms. And so they will be in white garments, that is, in the clarity of the flesh's innocence. And in the Gospel, the wedding garment sanctity of the flesh can be recognized. And so Isaiah, teaching what kind of fast the Lord has chosen, when he adds about the reward of goodness: Then, he says, your light will break forth, and your garments will arise more quickly: certainly not silk or a cloak, but wanting to accept the flesh, he predicted the rising of the flesh of the resurrection from the setting of death. So also an allegorical defense of the bodily resurrection is available to us. For also when we read: My people, enter into the inner rooms for a little while, until my anger passes, the inner rooms will be graves, in which those who have exceeded in the ends of the world, under the last anger, through the power of Antichrist, will rest for a little while. Or why was the word 'inner rooms' used rather than some receptacle place, unless because in the inner rooms the salted flesh is stored for use, to be brought out from there at its own time? For thus also the bodies, medicated with the spices of burial, are sequestered in sepulchers and monuments, to proceed from there when the Lord will have commanded. Which, when it is understood in this way, is consistent; and what refuges of storehouses will save us from the anger of God? by this very thing that it says, until the anger passes, which will extinguish Antichrist, after the anger it shows the flesh proceeding from the grave, in which it was placed before the anger. For also from the storehouses nothing else is brought out, than what is brought in; and after the eradication of Antichrist, the resurrection will be set in motion.

pass_b_english: We also have a mention of garments in Scripture that allegorizes the hope of the flesh, because the Apocalypse of John says: “These are the ones who have not defiled their garments with women” (Rev 14:4) —signifying virgins and those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. So they will be in white garments, that is, in the clarity of the flesh’s innocence. And in the Gospel the wedding garment can be recognized as the sanctity of the flesh. So Isaiah, teaching what kind of fast the Lord has chosen, when he adds the reward of goodness: “Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will spring up speedily” (Isa 58:8) —certainly not meaning silk or a cloak, but because he wants to accept the flesh, he predicted the rising of the flesh of the resurrection from the setting of death. So an allegorical defense of the bodily resurrection is available to us as well.

For when we read: “My people, enter your chambers and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the wrath has passed by” (Isa 26:20), the chambers will be graves in which those who have lived through the ends of the age, under the final wrath, through the power of Antichrist, will rest for a little while. Or why was the word ‘chambers’ used rather than some reception-place, unless because in the chambers the salted flesh is stored for use, to be brought out from there at its own time? For thus also the bodies, medicated with the spices of burial, are sequestered in sepulchers and monuments, to proceed from there when the Lord commands. Which, when understood this way, is consistent; and what refuges of storehouses will save us from the wrath of God? By this very thing that it says, ‘until the wrath passes,’ which will extinguish Antichrist, it shows the flesh proceeding from the grave after the wrath, in which it was placed before the wrath. For from storehouses nothing else is brought out than what was brought in; and after the eradication of Antichrist the resurrection will be set in motion.
